title: Party

jokes.text: Hank's audience warm-up: 'Now, first, you take off your clothes.'
jokes.setup: Hank is explaining to first-time audience members how a TV taping works, building earnest procedural expectation.
jokes.punchline: He instructs them to take off their clothes — a jarring non-sequitur that reveals his leering, performative personality.
jokes.explanation: A solid opener that efficiently establishes Hank's sleazy, self-important persona. The structure works — earnest setup followed by a non-sequitur that breaks expected procedure. It's a fairly stock 'emcee being inappropriate' joke but it's well-timed and character-specific to Hank's particular brand of grinning lechery.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Okay, ready? Now, first, you take off your clothes.

jokes.text: Hank squinting at the applause sign: 'Now, you see these applause signs... Or does that say "applesauce"?'
jokes.setup: Hank is instructing the audience on the applause signs, a routine warm-up moment.
jokes.punchline: He pretends to misread 'applause' as 'applesauce,' an absurd substitution that undercuts the whole enterprise.
jokes.explanation: A light, charming bit of Hank buffoonery. The word-swap joke is simple but 'applesauce' is a funny word choice — specific enough to feel fresh. It's not high craft, but it's economical and in-character for Hank's performative goofiness.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Or does that say 'applesauce'?

jokes.text: Larry to Jeannie, gesturing at his tie: 'This tie? You like it? Doesn't make my butt look fat, does it?'
jokes.setup: Larry is frantic backstage, 60 seconds to air, and his wife has appeared unexpectedly.
jokes.punchline: He deflects the pressure by asking if his tie makes his butt look fat — a non-sequitur that maps a classically female body-anxiety question onto a completely wrong garment.
jokes.explanation: This is sharp character work. The joke reveals Larry's vanity and anxiety all at once — he's preening under pressure, and the illogic of the question (a tie can't affect how your butt looks) is perfectly Shandling-esque. The delivery almost certainly carries deadpan panic, making this a character joke that doubles as absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This tie? You like it? Doesn't make my butt look fat, does it?

jokes.text: Stage manager says '40 seconds, Larry' and Larry echo-responds '40 seconds, Marty' — then someone says 'Better go find some good jokes.'
jokes.setup: Larry is 40 seconds from air, in the middle of a chaotic backstage moment.
jokes.punchline: The deadpan 'Better go find some good jokes' — implying he hasn't prepared adequately, delivered as a flat non-panicked observation.
jokes.explanation: A quick, dry institutional joke about the chaos of live TV production. Works as deadpan commentary on the whole show-business machinery. Not remarkable but economical and sets the right tone.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm going, 'Oh, jeez. Well, at least he's off the island.'

jokes.text: Larry's monologue: 'I haven't felt this up since last night.'
jokes.setup: Larry says 'All kidding aside, I haven't felt...' — the pause builds expectation for something warm or sincere.
jokes.punchline: '...this up since last night.' Deflates any sincerity with a non-punchline that essentially says nothing.
jokes.explanation: A quick anti-joke that subverts its own setup with a circular non-statement. It's the kind of throwaway monologue filler that feels authentic to real late-night writing — which is partly the point. The self-undermining structure fits Larry's performative confidence masking vacuity.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: The joke doesn't work unless he ends with the words 'adjustable beds.'

jokes.text: Larry's Gilligan/Bob Denver bit: '70 now... still wearing the red sweater and the sailor hat. At least he's off the island.'
jokes.setup: Larry sets up the Bob Denver commercial story — Gilligan, aged 70, doing ads for a boat shop on local cable.
jokes.punchline: 'At least he's off the island.' — a deflating joke that finds the one silver lining in the undignified spectacle.
jokes.explanation: A solid late-night observational joke. The structure is well-constructed — accumulating details (still in costume, 70 years old, local cable boat shop) before the sardonic release. The punchline is genuinely clever, turning a bleak image into a back-handed compliment. This is good functional monologue writing, slightly above average.

dialogue.line: Toilet monitor is busted, boys.

jokes.text: Larry flubs the Clinton/Lincoln bedroom joke — the punchline is 'water bed' instead of 'adjustable beds.'
jokes.setup: Larry tells a Bill Clinton joke about what changes he'd make at the White House — specifically in the Lincoln bedroom.
jokes.punchline: He says 'water bed' instead of 'adjustable beds,' killing the joke. The real joke IS the flub — we're watching a professional fail in real time.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent meta-comedy craft. The show deliberately writes a BAD joke (a joke within the show) that only lands properly when you hear the 'correct' version explained backstage — 'it doesn't work unless he ends with adjustable beds.' We see the flub, then hear the autopsy. The joke is simultaneously about Clinton, about late-night comedy writing, and about the gap between polished TV and the real mess behind it. The backstage explanation is the real punchline. Strong character integration — this is pure Larry, the flawed professional.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: She's halfway to her ideal weight, whatever that's supposed to mean.

jokes.text: Backstage: 'His timing really sucks tonight.' / 'He's off.' — while someone else says he's 'on' and 'very strong stuff.'
jokes.setup: Two groups are watching Larry from backstage — one group critiquing, one praising.
jokes.punchline: The simultaneous contradictory assessments play against each other — the pro says he's terrible; the civilian says he's incredible. The joke is the divergence.
jokes.explanation: Smart structural comedy — simultaneous contradicting assessments of Larry's performance create an ironic gap. The insiders who know him see the flub; his wife's circle is dazzled. It's a compressed version of the show's whole thesis about the gap between the TV product and the reality behind it. The editing does heavy lifting here.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You've never been to the house before?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Not that I recall. I have no mental picture.

jokes.text: A very funny monologue tonight. Yeah, he is on. This is as on as I've seen him in a long time. Very strong stuff. / [We just heard the writer say his timing sucks and he fucked up the Clinton joke]
jokes.setup: Artie and the writer have just skewered the monologue. We cut to Jeannie and another staffer watching the same performance.
jokes.punchline: They gush about how great it is — 'This is as on as I've seen him in a long time' — a complete tonal reversal.
jokes.explanation: Classic juxtaposition cut — the show uses scene structure as its punchline. The comedy is entirely in the edit: we've just been told he's bombing, and now people are swooning. Good craft through construction rather than dialogue. Rewatch bonus for the structural joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Your House? What is that, a new Chinese place?

jokes.text: The 'toilet monitor' — the group decides to go watch the show at the monitors by the toilet, and someone says 'Toilet monitor is busted, boys.'
jokes.setup: They casually agree to relocate to the 'toilet monitor' to watch the show, establishing that this is a normal thing.
jokes.punchline: 'Toilet monitor is busted, boys' — the absurdity of having a designated toilet-area monitor, now compounded by its being broken.
jokes.explanation: A great little production-world detail joke. The existence of a 'toilet monitor' is funny on its own — it suggests staff are so busy they watch the host on a monitor in the bathroom. Then it's broken. The economy is excellent; the absurd workplace-specific detail is exactly the kind of thing this show does well.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Be there or be square.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I can do both.

jokes.text: Artie, asked how Elaine is: 'She's halfway to her ideal weight, whatever that's supposed to mean.'
jokes.setup: A colleague makes small talk asking how Artie's wife Elaine is doing.
jokes.punchline: 'She's halfway to her ideal weight, whatever that's supposed to mean.' — a perfectly deadpan non-compliment delivered as an observation Artie genuinely doesn't understand.
jokes.explanation: This is a gem. Rip Torn's Artie is the perfect vessel for this line — a blunt, unsentimental man who genuinely doesn't process social niceties about women's bodies. 'Whatever that's supposed to mean' is the key: it's not a put-down, it's genuine bafflement, which makes it funnier and more specific than a simple insult. The line does three things at once: it characterizes Artie, it jokes about the absurdity of the 'ideal weight' concept, and it gets a laugh while being completely naturalistic. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's one person every two hours, half a person every hour.

jokes.text: Larry: 'What restaurant are we going to?' / Artie: 'Your house.' / Larry: 'Your House? What is that, a new Chinese place?'
jokes.setup: Artie tells Larry that Jeannie invited him to 'your house' for dinner. Larry has clearly not been briefed.
jokes.punchline: Larry responds as if 'Your House' is a restaurant name, specifically a Chinese restaurant — revealing simultaneously his social dissociation and his bewilderment.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first truly exceptional joke. The misdirection is elegant — 'your house' is grammatically ambiguous, but only someone as alienated from domestic life as Larry would genuinely process it as a restaurant name. The Chinese restaurant specification is the cherry: it's funny, specific, and reveals how Larry's mind works (he's always thinking restaurants, venues, public spaces). The two-beat follow-up ('No, it's your house, the place where you live') is a perfect straight-man line. This merits its 8+ because it's both a great joke AND a thesis statement about Larry's character.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: They're half salt, half vodka. Swear to God, the olive floats at the top.

jokes.text: Artie: 'The place I sleep in?' — Larry, confronted with the concept of his own home.
jokes.setup: Artie has just clarified 'your house, the place where you live.' Larry is still processing.
jokes.punchline: 'The place I sleep in?' — as if home is only identifiable by its most minimal function.
jokes.explanation: A terrific extension of the previous joke. Larry's conception of his own home as merely 'the place I sleep in' is both hilarious and quietly devastating. It deepens the character joke — Larry has reduced his domestic life to its lowest common denominator. The economy is near-perfect: five words that do enormous character work.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Has anyone ever been to Larry's house for dinner?
Not that I know of.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: That's weird. There must be a reason.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Be there or be square.' / Artie: 'I can do both.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to close the awkward dinner-planning conversation with an upbeat 'Be there or be square.'
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat 'I can do both' — a perfect deadpan that acknowledges his own squareness without defensiveness.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Artie lines in the episode. The comeback to a throwaway closing pleasantry is delivered with Artie's characteristic dry authority. It's self-aware without being cute about it — Artie genuinely IS square, and he's fine with that. The economy is exceptional: four words that perfectly cap a scene.

dialogue.speaker: Friend
dialogue.line: She's getting a promotion. Damn it!

jokes.text: Larry complains about having a dinner party: 'I'll be sitting on a couch, talking to people, entertaining... without being able to say, "We'll be right back."'
jokes.setup: Jeannie insists the dinner will be great. Larry is resistant, framing it as labor.
jokes.punchline: The inability to say 'We'll be right back' — as if the commercial break is the only socially acceptable way to escape human interaction, and he doesn't have that tool at home.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke and one of the series' defining lines. It perfectly encapsulates the show's central thesis: Larry Sanders has become so fused with his TV persona that he experiences real social interaction as a defective version of his show — one missing the escape valve of the commercial break. The 'We'll be right back' is such a specific, resonant detail that it illuminates Larry's entire psychology. High quotability, deep character integration, original comedic concept. Justifiably 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: These are vitamins.

jokes.text: Larry's math: 'Two people for four hours? That's one person every two hours, half a person every hour.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie says it's just 'one evening' with 'two people.' Larry tries to rationalize his anxiety with arithmetic.
jokes.punchline: He reduces guests to a rate — 'half a person every hour' — as if human social obligation is a unit of throughput.
jokes.explanation: A clever character moment. Larry's attempt to comfort himself by quantifying social exposure backfires — the math is technically correct but the framework is absurd. It reveals his clinical, performance-minded relationship to intimacy. Solid craft; the 'half a person every hour' image is particularly good.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey now! Well, I accept. I am... I'm very honored... and I would never miss a Larry Sanders event.

jokes.text: Larry on Artie's drinks: 'Don't let Artie make these drinks. They're half salt, half vodka. The olive floats at the top.'
jokes.setup: Larry is fretting about the dinner party logistics.
jokes.punchline: His specific anxiety about Artie's extreme martini proportions — the olive floating because the drink is essentially solid salt — is absurdly specific and characterizes Artie as an unreformed hard-drinking old-school TV man.
jokes.explanation: A good character detail joke. The image of the olive floating at the top of a drink that's more salt than liquid is funny and specific to Artie's hard-boiled persona. It's efficient shorthand for Artie's old-school excess without being cheap.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You tell her it's a big Larry Sanders shindig... a real time-of-your-life blowout. You tell her everybody's gonna be there.

jokes.text: Beverly's coworker: 'You cannot cancel Sister Circle for a man. That is such the reason that we even go there.' — then 'It's not a man. It's Larry.'
jokes.setup: Beverly is canceling her evening plans (Sister Circle, apparently a women's support group) to go to Larry's dinner as a 'buffer.'
jokes.punchline: The coworker says you can't cancel for a man — and Beverly's correction ('It's not a man. It's Larry.') implies Larry is something below or outside the category of 'man.'
jokes.explanation: A sharp little joke with good implicit bite. The line 'It's not a man. It's Larry' works on multiple levels — Larry as a category, Larry as a non-threatening entity, Larry as something requiring management rather than romance. The feminist sub-comedy of the Sister Circle context adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: I wasn't invited.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey. Hank'll make it right.

jokes.text: Beverly reveals she's going to Larry's house for dinner — coworker: 'Has anyone ever been to Larry's house for dinner?' / 'Not that I know of. That's weird. There must be a reason.'
jokes.setup: Beverly mentions Larry has invited her to his house for dinner.
jokes.punchline: The immediate office suspicion — no one has ever been there, so it must mean something. The conspiratorial 'there must be a reason' reframes a simple dinner invitation as a strange anomaly.
jokes.explanation: Reinforces the running joke about how closed-off Larry is domestically. The office gossip's conspiratorial reading of a dinner invitation is a nice comic beat — it turns Larry's social anxiety into a social legend. Good ensemble texture.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: As the talent booker, I work hands-on with the people. That's like a segment producer. To be blunt, she's like a glorified secretary.

jokes.text: Beverly is getting a promotion — coworker's reaction: 'She's getting a promotion. Damn it!'
jokes.setup: The coworkers are gossiping about Beverly being invited to the house. It suddenly registers that the dinner might be a promotion announcement.
jokes.punchline: 'Damn it!' — unguarded professional jealousy, blurted out without filter.
jokes.explanation: A quick, honest reaction-beat joke. The economy is excellent — the entire joke is one word. The nakedness of 'Damn it!' as a professional jealousy response is funny in its honesty, though it's not a sophisticated joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, shit. That fuckin' dinner. For once I try and join my personal life with my work life.

jokes.text: 'Are we still going to Sister Circle?' / 'Whatever!'
jokes.setup: Beverly has just bailed on Sister Circle — the whole point of which, they said, was not to cancel for men.
jokes.punchline: 'Whatever!' — the deflated, petulant response when the principle is immediately violated.
jokes.explanation: A quick callback payoff to the Sister Circle setup. The irony of the feminist solidarity group's plans collapsing the moment anyone gets a career opportunity is light but functional. 'Whatever' as a comedic punchline is low-craft but economically perfect here.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: I'm gonna bring my tarot cards tonight and do your wife.

jokes.text: Artie hears Beverly is being promoted and goes through a long, slow reaction beat: 'Beverly's being elevated?... Oh, yes, I remember... That's... interesting.'
jokes.setup: Someone mentions Beverly is being elevated/promoted, apparently something Artie and Larry discussed.
jokes.punchline: Artie's extended, measured response — he processes it slowly, confirms the memory, then settles on 'interesting' — a word that communicates volumes of professional skepticism without saying anything outright.
jokes.explanation: This is great Artie character comedy. The deliberate pacing — the pause, the 'we discussed that,' the 'that's... interesting' — is pure Rip Torn deadpan. 'Interesting' as a loaded non-word doing enormous work is a hallmark of this show's comedy of restraint. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing Artie's read of any situation tends to be more accurate than anyone else's.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: But just the tarot reading will be fine.

jokes.text: Hank's fake Holyfield-Bowe fight tickets — they turn out to be vitamins. 'These are vitamins. Please invite me to your party.'
jokes.setup: Hank enters dramatically with what he claims are two tickets to the Holyfield-Bowe fight. He teases revealing who he'd bring, building enormous suspense.
jokes.punchline: They're vitamins. He has no tickets. His pitch was pure theater to finagle a party invitation.
jokes.explanation: This is a superb piece of character comedy. Hank's entire gambit — the theatrical entrance, the sustained tension, the reveal of 'you' — is an elaborate con built on nothing. The vitamins reveal is both surprising and completely in character for a man who is always performing importance he doesn't actually have. 'Please invite me to your party' is a perfect, desperate, Hank-only line — the mask drops completely. Jeffrey Tambor's physical performance (inferred from the long pauses in the transcript) makes this even funnier. The structure earns its length.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Oh, Larry! What should I bring tonight? Ice? Chips? Salt!

jokes.text: Hank accepts the invitation: 'Hey now! Well, I accept. I am very honored and I would never miss a Larry Sanders event.'
jokes.setup: Larry belatedly invites Hank to the dinner, pretending he was going to invite him all along.
jokes.punchline: Hank accepts with grandiose ceremony — 'I would never miss a Larry Sanders event' — elevating a casual home dinner to a formal civic occasion, and revealing he was complicit in his own manipulation.
jokes.explanation: A good payoff to the vitamins scene. Hank's ceremonial acceptance of what was minutes ago a desperate plea is funny in its self-deception. 'A Larry Sanders event' is a great piece of Hank-speak — everything becomes a formal occasion when Hank is involved.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Phil, you know, I've got this... Ulcer? Party.

jokes.text: Excuse me. And Beverly can give me the address, right? / Beverly, give it to him. / I told you. We just talked about this.
jokes.setup: Hank, freshly invited, immediately makes an ask about the address, as if this is a legitimate business matter.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's exasperated 'I told you. We just talked about this' — Beverly has apparently already been having this conversation.
jokes.explanation: Small workplace irritation gag — Beverly's weariness with being Hank's keeper is a solid recurring undercurrent. Minor but textured.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: You're putting everything we own into a box.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Just a couple of things, like Aquarium Digest.

jokes.text: Give Shauna a buzz and see if she's free tonight. / Smoke House? / Oh, no. You tell her it's a big Larry Sanders shindig... a real time-of-your-life blowout. You tell her everybody's gonna be there.
jokes.setup: Hank has been invited to a small dinner party of two.
jokes.punchline: He immediately starts promoting it as 'a big Larry Sanders shindig... a real time-of-your-life blowout... everybody's gonna be there.' — turning a quiet dinner into a social event of national significance to lure a date.
jokes.explanation: Hank inflating a tiny event to grandiose proportions to impress a woman is perfectly character-specific. The gap between reality (quiet dinner for two) and his pitch ('time-of-your-life blowout') is the joke. Rewatch bonus — this inflation is exactly what then swells the party from 2 to 14 guests.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Then they'll decide we're not as happy as Burt Reynolds and Loni.

jokes.text: Beverly calls Jeannie back: 'Yeah, it's up to eight people.' / 'You better make that nine.' / 'Yeah, why don't we just say ten...'
jokes.setup: The headcount for the 'intimate' dinner has been climbing throughout the episode.
jokes.punchline: Beverly is now negotiating an ever-growing guest list with Larry's wife in real time — a dinner that was supposed to be for two couples is approaching catering territory.
jokes.explanation: A functional running-gag beat. The escalating headcount is the comic through-line of this act, and this moment efficiently advances it. Not a standalone great joke but does structural work in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: You do drink.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I do not drink.

jokes.text: The talent booker confronts Larry about Beverly's promotion — 'You don't have to say it. The dinner invitation kind of speaks volumes.'
jokes.setup: Larry was just trying to have a dinner party. Now it's been interpreted as a coded promotion announcement.
jokes.punchline: The talent booker has constructed an entire narrative from a dinner invitation — 'speaks volumes' — when it means nothing of the sort.
jokes.explanation: A good workplace cringe moment. The paranoid over-reading of a social invitation is very true to office politics, and it puts Larry in a characteristically impossible position. The comedy comes from the gap between intent (a dinner) and interpretation (a corporate announcement).

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Ooh, you're not my beautiful wife. Hey, hey, welcome. No dates?

jokes.text: Larry explodes: 'Oh, shit. That fuckin' dinner. For once I try and join my personal life with my work life. I am havin' fuckin' dinner. Jesus!'
jokes.setup: The talent booker has confronted Larry about Beverly's supposed promotion at his dinner party.
jokes.punchline: Larry's genuine exasperation at what his innocent dinner has become — a string of profanity that captures his full neurotic helplessness.
jokes.explanation: A good venting-frustration beat. Larry's exasperation is earned by the accumulated misreadings of the dinner party, and 'For once I try and join my personal life with my work life' is genuinely funny in its self-pity. The profanity works as comic punctuation. Not a crafted joke so much as a character explosion.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: It is! You cry every time at the end... when he finishes with his mission on Earth and has to go back to heaven.

jokes.text: Larry to the booker: 'In my own unique way, I was trying to invite you... to what I believe will be a very fun dinner.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just screamed at the talent booker. He now does a full about-face to invite her to the dinner he didn't want.
jokes.punchline: 'In my own unique way' — a masterpiece of passive self-description that acknowledges his behavior was bizarre without taking any real responsibility for it.
jokes.explanation: 'In my own unique way' is a great Larry Sanders line — utterly self-serving, delivered with complete sincerity, and a masterclass in non-apology language. It's character comedy that doubles as a meditation on how narcissistic men describe their own bad behavior. The follow-up 'what I believe will be a very fun dinner' is a perfect euphemism for the disaster we know is coming.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Just because Cheers was a hit, every asshole thinks he can mix a drink.

jokes.text: Beverly reports the count is up to 12 — Jeannie suggests 14 to be safe — Larry: 'Would you not invite any more people? Jeez, it's my dinner. It's my house, my sofa.'
jokes.setup: The intimate dinner has grown to 12, possibly 14 people. Larry is losing control of his own party.
jokes.punchline: 'It's my house, my sofa' — the mounting desperation culminating in the specific detail of claiming ownership of furniture.
jokes.explanation: A good escalation beat. 'My sofa' is a funny specific detail — you don't usually claim ownership of furniture in a dinner-party dispute, which makes it funny. Larry's shrinking claim of authority (house → sofa) is a nice diminuendo.

dialogue.line: No, Larry paid for it.
Cost him a few thousand dollars too.
A few thousand dollars?
That's right.
It's not that funny.

jokes.text: Beverly: 'Right. Larry Sanders has spoken.' (after Larry asserts it's his house and sofa)
jokes.setup: Larry has just issued his decree about the dinner.
jokes.punchline: 'Larry Sanders has spoken' — Beverly's dry third-person proclamation mocks his authority while appearing to respect it.
jokes.explanation: A quick efficient jab from Beverly. The third-person mock-deference is a reliable comic structure, well-executed here. It efficiently captures the power dynamic between the star and his staff.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I wrote some party jokes for you to use throughout the night.

jokes.text: Darlene: 'I'm gonna bring my tarot cards tonight and do your wife.' — Larry: 'But just the tarot reading will be fine.'
jokes.setup: Darlene announces excitedly that she'll bring her tarot cards to 'do' Larry's wife.
jokes.punchline: Larry's clarification 'But just the tarot reading will be fine' implies he had to specify that Darlene shouldn't do anything else to his wife — a mild double entendre that characterizes Darlene as a slightly unhinged enthusiast.
jokes.explanation: A clean minor joke. The double-meaning of 'do your wife' is gently exploited, and Larry's anxious clarification adds character texture. It's not a standout moment but it's efficient and in-character.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: I said no, so we ended up dry-humping on the couch all week. He's an animal.

jokes.text: Phil calls asking what to bring to 'tonight' — Larry hasn't told Phil about the party, so he panics — Phil guesses 'Ulcer?'
jokes.setup: Larry says 'Phil, you know, I've got this...' starting to deflect.
jokes.punchline: Phil guesses 'Ulcer?' — a knowing joke about Larry's chronic anxiety that lands as both sympathetic and absurd.
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean joke. The gap between Larry's attempted excuse and Phil's completion of it — 'Ulcer?' — is funny because Phil knows Larry so well that he finishes his deflections. It also enriches Larry's characterization as a congenitally anxious person.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: Then, of course, that night he wanted to have sex. I said no, so we ended up dry-humping on the couch all week.

jokes.text: Hello. / Oh, Larry! What should I bring tonight? Ice? Chips? Salt!
jokes.setup: Larry tries to shut down further invitations; his phone rings immediately.
jokes.punchline: It's Phil, already excitedly planning his contribution: 'Ice? Chips? Salt!' — the rapid-fire enthusiasm and the oddness of 'Salt!' as a bringing-to-a-party item is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The 'Salt!' specifically pays off the Salty Dog setup — it's the most specific and funniest option Phil offers. Also continues the running 'party out of control' escalation. The escalating list lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hey, would you mind using the bathroom downstairs?

jokes.text: Larry's pre-party anxiety: 'I don't want Martin Mull to come over to see what's going on. I hate the way he's always gotta know what's going on.'
jokes.setup: Larry is worried about keeping the party quiet.
jokes.punchline: His specific anxiety is about neighbor Martin Mull — a real celebrity, name-dropped as a nosy neighbor. The joke is that this is a completely petty and specific paranoia.
jokes.explanation: A mild celebrity-name joke with light comedy from the specificity of Larry's paranoia. The joke is that Martin Mull as a nosy neighbor is hilariously mundane. It sets up the later actual Martin Mull appearance, giving it a rewatch bonus in hindsight.

dialogue.speaker: Martin
dialogue.line: Just saw more than one car, so I got to thinking... 'That's not right.'

jokes.text: You're putting everything we own into a box. / Just a couple of things, like Aquarium Digest. / I don't think they need to know this kind of information.
jokes.setup: Larry is pre-emptively hiding personal items from the guests. Jeannie catches him.
jokes.punchline: 'Just a couple of things, like Aquarium Digest' — the specific magazine is funnier than any generic choice could be.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Aquarium Digest' is excellent comedy writing — you couldn't predict it, it's completely benign, and yet Larry treats it as intelligence material. It also characterizes Larry as the kind of man who reads Aquarium Digest, which is perfect. The joke is entirely in the specific noun.

dialogue.speaker: Martin
dialogue.line: Didn't scrimp on anything, did ya?

jokes.text: Larry: 'You'll see they poke around like it's some museum. Then they'll decide we're not as happy as Burt Reynolds and Loni. That's all I'm gonna be hearing.'
jokes.setup: Larry is justifying hiding personal items before the party.
jokes.punchline: The specific comparison to Burt Reynolds and Loni Anderson — a celebrity couple — as the benchmark of happiness is absurd, and 'that's all I'm gonna be hearing' suggests this is a familiar refrain.
jokes.explanation: A clever showbiz-world joke. The fact that Larry's happiness benchmark is Burt Reynolds and Loni Anderson — a celebrity couple who would notoriously divorce — is a rich irony available to contemporary viewers. 'That's all I'm gonna be hearing' adds a domestic-comedy texture.

dialogue.speaker: Martin
dialogue.line: Instead of saying, 'Hey now!'... you'd say, 'Come here!'

jokes.text: Larry refuses a drink before the party: 'They'll smell it on my breath, and they'll think that I drink.' / 'You do drink.' / 'You do. I do not drink.'
jokes.setup: Larry's housekeeper offers him a drink before the party.
jokes.punchline: Larry refuses because he doesn't want guests to smell it — Jeannie points out he does drink — Larry denies it, contradicting himself in the same breath ('You do. I do not drink.').
jokes.explanation: A nicely structured three-beat joke. The internal contradiction ('You do. I do not drink') is classic Larry self-delusion. It reveals his image management extends even to his own behavior when no one is watching — he's performing for an imagined audience at all times.

dialogue.speaker: Martin
dialogue.line: That is what you can use if the show goes off the air.

jokes.text: Larry: 'You know, I'm the one who should be nervous. I don't even know these people, and I am relaxed. Goody for you.'
jokes.setup: Jeannie points out she should be more nervous than Larry since she doesn't know the work guests. Larry agrees — 'Goody for you' — with barely concealed contempt.
jokes.punchline: 'Goody for you' — a magnificently passive-aggressive response that ends the exchange.
jokes.explanation: 'Goody for you' is a perfect passive-aggressive phrase — technically positive, actually withering. It's economically delivered and completely in character for a man who is silently furious about the dinner but can't directly admit it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: You were spying on me?

jokes.text: Larry panics about the medicine chest: 'Hello. Did you clean out the medicine chest?' — he never checks if it's been done, just panics about it.
jokes.setup: Last-minute pre-party anxiety checklist.
jokes.punchline: The medicine chest is apparently a trove of embarrassing or private information — the fact that this is the last thing Larry checks suggests it's his most anxious concern about guests snooping.
jokes.explanation: A quick beat extending the 'hiding his life' running theme. The medicine chest is a classic party-hosting anxiety trope — people DO snoop — and Larry's panic about it is consistent with his character. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.line: It's a toga. Must be a white thing.

jokes.text: Artie and his date arrive separately from their 'dates' — Artie was having Chinese, his companion was watching Ghost — they meet on the doorstep having come from different places.
jokes.setup: Larry greets what he thinks are a couple arriving together.
jokes.punchline: 'We were having Chinese.' / 'We were watching Ghost.' — they weren't together; they arrived simultaneously from completely separate evenings, with no explanation.
jokes.explanation: A good dry arrival gag. The mundane specificity of their separate pre-party activities ('Chinese' / 'Ghost') and the casual delivery — as if this is totally normal — is a nice piece of dry comedy. It suggests a marriage with very separate domestic lives, which is both a joke and a thematic mirror for Larry and Jeannie.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Drink it, you pussy.

jokes.text: Ooh, you're not my beautiful wife. [to arriving guest]
jokes.setup: Larry opens the door expecting Jeannie, finds a colleague.
jokes.punchline: 'Ooh, you're not my beautiful wife' — reflexive, borderline-inappropriate greeting delivered with total naturalness.
jokes.explanation: Nicely awkward door-opening moment. The 'ooh' of disappointment followed by the compliment-to-absent-wife is a small, natural cringe. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: The thing is, see, our coats? Yeah? They're in the bedroom... and, well, the bedroom door is locked.

jokes.text: We were having Chinese. — We were watching Ghost.
jokes.setup: Artie and Elaine arrive; someone asks what they were doing before
jokes.punchline: Their two simultaneous, contradictory explanations — 'having Chinese' vs. 'watching Ghost' — reveals a marriage where neither party knows what the other was doing, or they were doing both and disagree on the priority
jokes.explanation: Quiet but effective. The contradiction in two words per character sketches a whole marriage dynamic. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I never put my keys in the bedroom, in case someone gets in a sleepy mood.

jokes.text: Artie says Ghost is Larry's favorite movie — Jeannie confirms he cries at the end 'when he finishes with his mission on Earth and has to go back to heaven' — Larry denies it but immediately needs to go to the bar.
jokes.setup: Larry dismisses Ghost as his favorite film.
jokes.punchline: Jeannie's overly specific description of the ending ('finishes with his mission on Earth and has to go back to heaven') reveals she knows exactly which part makes him cry, and Larry's denial followed by an abrupt exit to the bar is the reaction beat.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sweet and funny character moment. The joke works on multiple levels: Larry's fragile masculinity, Jeannie's affectionate exposure of it, and the specific description of the Ghost ending (which is earnest and slightly absurd) all land together. Larry's abrupt 'Bar's this way?' escape is the perfect physical punctuation. This is character comedy at its most economical and revealing.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Five marriages.

jokes.text: Artie about the kid bartender: 'Just because Cheers was a hit, every asshole thinks he can mix a drink.'
jokes.setup: The bartender has made Salty Dogs with wrong proportions.
jokes.punchline: Artie attributes all bad amateur bartending to the cultural influence of Cheers — an industry-insider joke that is both absurdly reductive and completely Artie.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Artie's theory that Cheers ruined amateur bartending is a perfectly calibrated industry-insider joke — the right level of absurdity (blaming a TV show for a cultural phenomenon), the right level of sourness (Artie's contempt for pop-culture influence), and the right economy (one sentence). 'Every asshole thinks he can mix a drink' is a great turn of phrase. This is exactly the kind of throwaway line that defines a character. Justifies 8+ because it's the kind of line that gets quoted out of context and still lands.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Now I'm going downstairs and I'm gonna take care of that... sack of human shit with a camera.

jokes.text: The Martin Mull painting: guests notice it, ask if he gave it to Larry — 'No, Larry paid for it. Cost him a few thousand dollars.' / 'A few thousand dollars?' / 'It's not that funny.'
jokes.setup: Guests are admiring/assessing a painting on the wall. They wonder if the celebrity neighbor gave it to Larry as a gift.
jokes.punchline: Larry paid full price. 'It's not that funny' — his defensive response to their implied amusement confirms there IS something funny about it.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed joke. The social dynamic — guests assessing whether art was gifted or purchased — is very real and funny. Larry's 'It's not that funny' is a classic over-denial that confirms his embarrassment about having paid thousands for art by his neighbor.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: One of those little Lady Di smiles.

jokes.text: Is that a Martin Mull painting? / Yeah, it is. / Do you think he gave it to Larry? / No, Larry paid for it. Cost him a few thousand dollars too. / A few thousand dollars? / That's right. / It's not that funny.
jokes.setup: Two guests discover a Martin Mull painting on Larry's wall and speculate whether it was a gift.
jokes.punchline: The news that Larry paid several thousand dollars for it provokes laughter from the guests, capped by the defender's 'It's not that funny' — which confirms it is funny.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the Mull appearance. The guests' instinct to laugh at Larry overpaying for a painting by his neighbor, combined with the flustered 'it's not that funny,' is naturalistic workplace-party comedy. Rewatch bonus when Mull appears and turns out to be exactly as depicted.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'll bet Letterman fights with that woman who claims to be his wife.

jokes.text: Hank surprises Larry with written party jokes: 'I wrote some party jokes for you to use throughout the night.' / 'You wrote some party jokes?' / 'Yes.' / 'That's ridiculous.'
jokes.setup: Hank pulls out a prepared set of jokes for Larry to use at his own dinner party.
jokes.punchline: Larry's incredulous 'That's ridiculous' — but Hank insists. The idea that a man needs scripted jokes for his own home is both an insult and, given what we know about Larry, almost true.
jokes.explanation: An excellent Hank joke that doubles as Larry character commentary. Hank writing party jokes for Larry is both presumptuous and accidentally perceptive — given Larry's anxiety about socializing without a 'We'll be right back' safety net, he might actually need them. The joke earns its craft score through deep character integration: it simultaneously characterizes Hank as enabling/obsequious and Larry as genuinely dependent on performance scaffolding.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Great party. Great. It was great.

jokes.text: Jeannie tells the Aspen story: 'Then, of course, that night he wanted to have sex. I said no, so we ended up dry-humping on the couch all week.'
jokes.setup: Guests have asked for the romantic story of how Larry and Jeannie met in Aspen.
jokes.punchline: 'We ended up dry-humping on the couch all week.' — Jeannie delivers the punchline to a wholesome meet-cute story with casual, cheerful oversharing that horrifies Larry.
jokes.explanation: A standout joke. The setup is a perfect romantic-comedy structure — meeting on a T-bar, asking her out the first night — and the overshare punchline is perfectly timed and shockingly specific. 'Dry-humping on the couch all week' is funny because of the precision (all week), the casual delivery, and the complete social inappropriateness. It also perfectly characterizes Jeannie as the character who doesn't perform for guests the way Larry does — she just tells the truth, which is the thing Larry fears most. High marks for structure, character integration, and earned comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Great party. Great. It was great.

jokes.text: Larry: 'That is not... I am an animal. I'm an animal, huh, Artie? I'm an animal.' — seeking Artie's endorsement of his masculinity.
jokes.setup: After Jeannie's dry-humping revelation, Larry simultaneously denies and embraces being 'an animal.'
jokes.punchline: Larry turning to Artie for validation — 'I'm an animal, huh, Artie?' — is a perfect social panic reaction, seeking masculine confirmation from the least likely source.
jokes.explanation: A great reaction beat. Larry's split-second recalibration — from denial to embrace of 'animal' status — and his turn to Artie for confirmation is perfectly calibrated insecurity. Artie's presumably deadpan 'Definitely an animal' closes the loop beautifully.

jokes.text: I gotta pee real bad. / Hey, would you mind using the bathroom downstairs?
jokes.setup: Artie announces a biological need with total candor at a party.
jokes.punchline: Larry's reflexive 'would you mind using the bathroom downstairs?' — the host-anxiety of directing guests away from the private medicine-cabinet-holding upstairs bathroom, even for a pee request.
jokes.explanation: Callbacks to the medicine chest and box-hiding paranoia. Larry's immediate protective instinct even for a bathroom visit is a good character beat — his home is still the show, and every room is stage-managed.

jokes.text: Martin Mull actually shows up — he saw the cars. 'I just saw more than one car, so I got to thinking, "That's not right."'
jokes.setup: Larry had specifically worried about Martin Mull being a nosy neighbor before the party. Now he's literally at the door.
jokes.punchline: Martin Mull's stated reason for coming over — he saw more than one car and found that suspicious — is both absurdly nosy and hilariously self-aware.
jokes.explanation: An excellent callback payoff. Larry's pre-party paranoia about Martin Mull proved completely accurate — he showed up because he saw cars. The specific logic ('more than one car... that's not right') is funny because it's so intensely nosy disguised as civic concern. The meta-layer of Martin Mull playing a version of himself as Larry's intrusive neighbor is a sharp showbiz joke.

jokes.text: Martin Mull to Hank on 'Hey now': 'Which writer came up with "Hey now"?' / 'Hank did.' / 'It's brilliant. Really!'
jokes.setup: Mull tells Hank the origin story of 'Hey now' — asking if he ever thought about changing it.
jokes.punchline: Mull calls 'Hey now' brilliant — which is either sincere (absurdly over-crediting a catchphrase) or sarcastic (gently mocking it). Either way Hank beams.
jokes.explanation: A nice meta-joke about catchphrases. The idea of 'Hey now' as a brilliant creative achievement is funny in its inflation, and the scene allows Hank a moment of genuine pride in what is, essentially, two words he strung together.

jokes.text: Have you ever thought about changing it? / No. / Just listen to this, okay? [pause] Instead of saying 'Hey now!'... you'd say, 'Come here!'
jokes.setup: Having praised 'Hey now,' Mull immediately pitches a replacement.
jokes.punchline: With enormous buildup and theatrical suspense, Mull's alternative is... 'Come here.' — a completely random, incoherent replacement delivered as a major contribution.
jokes.explanation: The best absurdist joke in the episode. Mull builds enormous suspense ('Just listen to this, okay? [beat]') and the punchline is 'Come here' — which is not only not better than 'Hey now,' it makes no sense as a catchphrase at all. The gap between the buildup and the content is perfectly calibrated. Then Hank trying it out and people reacting as if it's working completes the joke beautifully. Martin Mull's character — the artist who is both brilliant and completely untethered from usefulness — is perfectly deployed.

jokes.text: Mull's aside about 'Come here' being for when the show goes off the air — Larry overhears and panics: 'What do you mean, when the show...'
jokes.setup: Mull casually drops that 'Come here' is what Hank can use 'if the show goes off the air.' Larry immediately overhears.
jokes.punchline: Larry's spiral: 'What show goes off the air?' / Jeannie mentions Montana / 'She's kidding.' / 'No. Really.' — and Larry has to drag Jeannie away.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant escalation. What began as an absurdist catchphrase bit turns into a catastrophic public airing of Larry's private anxieties — the Montana plan (his possible exit from the business) is now party small talk. Larry's panic is perfectly calibrated, and Jeannie's genuine 'No. Really.' is a devastating straight line. The scene captures the whole episode's theme: Larry cannot control what information gets out when his work and personal worlds collide.

jokes.text: She's not well. Excuse us.
jokes.setup: Jeannie has just revealed Larry's Montana plans to everyone. Larry needs to extract her.
jokes.punchline: 'She's not well. Excuse us.' — Larry retroactively pathologizing his wife's honesty as illness.
jokes.explanation: Four words of maximum efficiency. 'She's not well' as a cover story for a wife who said something true is a great defensive maneuver. Very Larry — he manages his wife like a guest who went off-script.

jokes.text: Larry confronts Jeannie: 'You're telling people about our lives. About dry-humping, Aspen, Montana.' / 'You were spying on me?' / 'I was standing nearby.'
jokes.setup: Larry has pulled Jeannie aside after the Montana revelation.
jokes.punchline: Jeannie's 'You were spying on me?' / Larry's 'I was standing nearby.' — a perfect semantic distinction that captures Larry's inability to admit his own behavior.
jokes.explanation: A quietly devastating exchange. 'I was standing nearby' as a distinction from 'spying' is perfect Larry — always technically accurate, never honest. The economy is excellent: the entire fight is compressed into this one semantic quibble. Earns its craft score through deep character integration.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I just want you to be yourself.' / Jeannie: 'I am being myself.' / Larry: 'I will tell you when I am being myself.'
jokes.setup: Larry tells Jeannie he wants her to be herself.
jokes.punchline: Jeannie says she is — and Larry corrects her: 'I will tell you when I am being myself.' A completely self-defeating line that reveals he believes he controls her authenticity.
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke and one of the series' finest lines. 'I will tell you when I am being myself' is a profound comic mistake — Larry means to say 'I will tell you when YOU are being yourself' but says 'I' instead, which is either a Freudian slip (revealing he doesn't know when he's genuine) or a control-freak assertion (he'll define her authenticity for her). Either reading is devastating and funny. It's the entire episode's thesis about Larry's inability to separate performance from reality compressed into one sentence. Perfect economy, unbeatable character integration, deeply original. Justifies 8+ by being the kind of line that reveals a character's entire psychology in ten words.

jokes.text: Jeannie: 'Excuse me. I'm from Chicago. When we have parties, we invite actual friends and we have fun. And we talk about whatever comes up.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to manage what Jeannie says at the party.
jokes.punchline: Jeannie's 'I'm from Chicago' as an explanation for basic human social behavior — as if normal friendship is a regional custom Larry isn't familiar with.
jokes.explanation: A strong line. 'I'm from Chicago' as a preface to 'we invite actual friends' is a sharp implicit critique — Larry's Hollywood world has made normal friendship into a performance art, and Jeannie calls it out with geographical bluntness. The joke works as character contrast and social observation simultaneously.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Keep it down. They will think we're fighting.' / Jeannie: 'We ARE fighting!'
jokes.setup: Larry and Jeannie are having a heated argument in a side room at the party.
jokes.punchline: Larry's priority is that no one hears them fighting — Jeannie's explosive 'We ARE fighting!' is the obvious response to the absurdity of managing the appearance of a fight while having it.
jokes.explanation: A classic marital-comedy structure executed well. The joke isn't novel — 'stop fighting so they don't hear us fighting' is a familiar premise — but it's executed with precision and is perfectly character-specific. Larry's obsession with appearance over reality is at its most absurd here.

jokes.text: Guests find the toga photo: 'Must be a white thing.' / Larry: 'No, I don't get it either. It's a stupid thing.'
jokes.setup: Guests have discovered the toga photo Larry tried to hide. A guest (presumably Black) attributes it to white cultural customs.
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'No, I don't get it either. It's a stupid thing.' — he disavows his own youthful behavior to fit in with the guests' bemusement.
jokes.explanation: A good callback payoff. The toga photo that Jeannie wanted to leave out (calling it adorable) has now become a social problem for exactly the reasons Larry feared. His immediate disavowal of toga parties is both self-serving and funny. The racial-cultural observation is handled lightly.

jokes.text: Someone is filming the party without permission. Two characters react: 'What the... Get out!' and 'as soon as I finish this Salty Dog, I'm gonna rip that camera from his hands and tear him a new A-hole.'
jokes.setup: An uninvited cameraman has appeared at the party.
jokes.punchline: Artie's measured threat: he will absolutely deal with this — but first he needs to finish his drink. The specificity of 'Salty Dog' as the delay makes it hilarious.
jokes.explanation: A great Artie moment. The threat to 'tear him a new A-hole' is vintage Rip Torn, but the comedy comes from the qualifier — he'll do this after finishing his Salty Dog. The callback to Artie's extreme bartending standards (half salt, half vodka) adds resonance. Artie's violence is always deferred just enough to be funny rather than alarming.

jokes.text: Larry to Artie about women: 'I don't understand women.' / Artie: 'I agree. Here. Have a Salty Dog.' / Larry: 'No, I—' / Artie: 'Drink it, you pussy.'
jokes.setup: Larry is upset about his fight with Jeannie and confesses he doesn't understand women.
jokes.punchline: 'Drink it, you pussy.' — Artie's prescription for Larry's emotional distress is a Salty Dog delivered with a contemptuous command.
jokes.explanation: An excellent Artie line. 'Drink it, you pussy' is perfect character comedy — Artie's emotional toolkit is entirely composed of alcohol and contempt, deployed here with genuine affection. The economy is superb: four words that capture the entire Artie/Larry dynamic. The Salty Dog callback and the role reversal (Artie was refusing to let people bartend for him earlier) adds texture. Justifies high score through perfect character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Hank tries to excuse Shauna leaving early: 'It's just that, you know, Shauna's a little tired.' / Artie: 'That is something more than tired, Hank.' / Hank: 'She's overtired.'
jokes.setup: Shauna wants to leave and Hank is making excuses.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'That is something more than tired, Hank' — implying Shauna has had a visible breakdown of some kind — and Hank's escalation to 'overtired' as a solution.
jokes.explanation: A very good deadpan exchange. Artie's clinical 'something more than tired' is funny because it's so measured about what is clearly a visible meltdown, and Hank's immediate escalation to 'overtired' — as if the solution is just a more intense version of tired — is perfect Hank coping-mechanism comedy.

jokes.text: No, no. I had a lovely time. It's just that, you know, Shauna's a little tired... / That is something more than tired, Hank. / She's overtired. / Yes. Yeah.
jokes.setup: Hank's date Shauna is apparently in bad shape. Hank covers with 'tired.'
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'That is something more than tired' and Hank's escalation: 'She's overtired.' — the euphemism upgrade is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Overtired' as the ratcheted-up euphemism for whatever state Shauna is actually in is a tight, elegant escalation. The word 'overtired' used for adults with a straight face is inherently funny. Good economy and character-specific (Hank's desperate face-saving).

jokes.text: Hank and his date can't get their coats — Jeannie has locked herself in the bedroom. 'The thing is, see, our coats? They're in the bedroom... and, well, the bedroom door is locked.'
jokes.setup: Hank wants to leave but his coats are trapped behind a locked door.
jokes.punchline: The mundane coat-retrieval problem has become a hostage situation because of the marital crisis. The absurdity of coat logistics driving the scene is very funny.
jokes.explanation: Good structural cringe comedy. The coats-in-the-locked-bedroom problem is a perfect comic complication — the marital crisis has literally trapped the guests. The formality of Hank explaining the situation to Larry ('the bedroom door is locked') when Larry obviously knows is a nice uncomfortable beat.

jokes.text: Hank's explanation of Jeannie's behavior escalates: 'She was... She wasn't even in there. But she's crying. She is... has fallen asleep.'
jokes.setup: Hank reports on Jeannie's status behind the locked door.
jokes.punchline: His rapid reinterpretation — crying → fallen asleep — is clearly a cover story constructed in real time, with each version more implausible than the last.
jokes.explanation: Good Hank improvisation comedy. The rapid cover-story revisions — she's not there / she's crying / she's asleep — track Hank's real-time damage control with perfect comic escalation. It characterizes Hank as a loyal but terrible crisis manager.

jokes.text: Guest leaving without coat: 'I didn't even like that coat.' / Larry: 'No, I'll get that stuff.' / Guest: 'Except car keys.' / Larry: 'I never put my keys in the bedroom, in case someone gets in a sleepy mood.'
jokes.setup: Guests are trying to leave but their belongings are trapped in the bedroom.
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'I never put my keys in the bedroom, in case someone gets in a sleepy mood' — a new household rule invented on the spot to explain why he, unlike his guests, has his keys.
jokes.explanation: A very good line. 'In case someone gets in a sleepy mood' is a beautifully euphemistic way to describe his wife having a crisis and locking herself in the bedroom. It's a brand-new household policy delivered as a longstanding wisdom, and the specific 'sleepy mood' framing is both absurd and specific to Larry's image-management style.

jokes.text: 'I didn't want my keys anyway.' / 'It's better this way.' / 'No, it's not better this way. This is bullshit. I want my coat.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to frame the coat situation as somehow positive.
jokes.punchline: 'No, it's not better this way. This is bullshit. I want my coat.' — the guest's patience snaps, and the pretense that this is acceptable collapses.
jokes.explanation: A good escalation beat. The pretense finally collapses — 'this is bullshit' is satisfying because the situation has been increasingly untenable, and the mundane specificity of 'I want my coat' as the crisis-point is funny.

jokes.text: 'She's your wife. Could you go in there, tell her to open the goddamn door?' — Artie's five-marriage context immediately follows.
jokes.setup: A guest demands Larry get Jeannie to open the door.
jokes.punchline: Artie follows this with 'Five marriages.' — volunteering his marital résumé as context for why he knows this won't work.
jokes.explanation: Two words — 'Five marriages.' — that do everything. Artie volunteers his qualifications for having an opinion on locked-bedroom marital standoffs, and the number is both a joke (it's a lot of marriages) and a revelation (Artie has been here before, many times). The economy is near-perfect, the character integration is excellent (only Artie would cite this as credential), and the timing — landing right after the demand that Larry handle his wife — is superb.

jokes.text: Artie tries to get Jeannie to open the door: 'Jeannie, the last thing this house needs... is tough love. Jeannie, open this door!'
jokes.setup: Artie, who just said 'Five marriages,' now attempts to coax Jeannie out.
jokes.punchline: His approach: first, sympathetically say the house doesn't need 'tough love' — then immediately deploy tough love: 'Jeannie, open this door!' The self-contradiction delivered in consecutive sentences is perfectly Artie.
jokes.explanation: An excellent joke that earns its 8+ score. Artie's two-sentence contradiction — explicitly rejecting tough love, then immediately employing it — is perfectly structured and deeply character-specific. No one else on this show could deliver this. The 'five marriages' setup makes it even funnier: this is how he approaches emotional situations. The escalation from gentle to commanding in a single breath is superb writing.

jokes.text: Five marriages.
jokes.setup: Artie's tough love fails to open the door. A beat of silence.
jokes.punchline: Artie says simply: 'Five marriages.' — delivered as an explanation for why he knows about bedroom standoffs.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. Two words. The economy is flawless — it is simultaneously a confession, an explanation, a joke, and a character revelation. We don't need to hear about any of the five marriages. The number is the punchline. It explains why he pronounced against tough love (experience) and why tough love failed (also experience). Artie's entire life outside the show is compressed into two syllables. This is what a great 9 looks like — maximum information at minimum cost, and it illuminates a character indelibly.

jokes.text: Larry and Jeannie fight in whispers — 'All you care about is what they think.' / 'That is not true.' / 'Then why are you whispering?' / 'I am not whispering.'
jokes.setup: They're now fighting about whether Larry is whispering to hide their fight.
jokes.punchline: He denies whispering while whispering — the denial IS the evidence. Perfect self-incrimination.
jokes.explanation: One of the finest jokes in the episode, and close to the series' best. 'Then why are you whispering?' / 'I am not whispering' is structurally impeccable — the denial performed in the very manner it denies is a self-contained logical loop. It captures the entire episode's theme (Larry's self-delusion about image vs. reality) in a four-word exchange. The structure is nearly perfect: setup creates the trap, punchline springs it. This is the kind of joke that works equally well on the page and in performance. Justifies 8.5+ because it's both a great standalone joke and a perfect thematic capsule.

jokes.text: Larry asks Jeannie for 'one of those little Lady Di smiles' to wave the guests out — 'That's all I'm asking from you. Okay. One more fake moment and we're done.'
jokes.setup: The guests are leaving and Larry needs a performance from Jeannie for the send-off.
jokes.punchline: 'One more fake moment and we're done' — Larry reduces his marriage to a series of performed moments, now bargaining for just one more with theatrical precision.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional line. 'One more fake moment and we're done' is devastating and funny simultaneously — the casual professionalism with which Larry treats his marriage as a performance is perfectly rendered. The 'Lady Di smile' reference is specific and sad: a performance of gracious suffering. This line earns 8+ because it's both a great joke and the episode's thematic apex — Larry explicitly asking his wife to perform happiness for their guests while acknowledging it's fake.

jokes.text: Larry's parting shot to the camera/audience: 'All right. So we're fighting, okay? That's it. What, you don't... You think we're the only ones who fight? Everybody fights. Everybody has fights. I'll bet Letterman fights with that woman who claims to be his wife.'
jokes.setup: Larry addresses the camera/guests after the party disaster, trying to normalize what happened.
jokes.punchline: 'I'll bet Letterman fights with that woman who claims to be his wife.' — the industry-insider dig at Letterman's infamously cold domestic life, delivered as universal solidarity.
jokes.explanation: A terrific closing joke. 'That woman who claims to be his wife' is both the dig and the structure — it mirrors Larry's own situation (wife locked in bedroom, marriage in crisis) while projecting it onto a real industry rival. Larry using Letterman as a comfort object is character-specific and meta. The line is quotable and reveals Larry's competitive relationship with his late-night peers.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I don't care what you think. I love my wife. I don't care. I love my wife and I don't care what you think!' — screamed at departing guests.
jokes.setup: Larry has been defending his marriage, spiraling into increasingly emphatic declarations.
jokes.punchline: The repetition — 'I don't care... I love my wife... I don't care... I love my wife' — escalates past sincerity into performance, the declaration becoming more performative with each iteration.
jokes.explanation: A great escalation beat. Larry's sincere declaration devolves into shouted theater — he's performing 'man who loves his wife' for guests who are already gone. The self-undermining structure of the scene (declaring you don't care while obviously caring enormously) is pure Larry Sanders.

jokes.text: Morning, Larry. / Morning. Morning. / Hi, Larry. / Good morning. / Great party. / Great. It was great.
jokes.setup: Next morning at the show. Staff greet Larry with 'Great party!'
jokes.punchline: Larry's dead, flat 'Great. It was great.' — the show-must-go-on end-note on a disastrous evening.
jokes.explanation: A clean, professional button on the episode. Larry's hollow 'Great. It was great' after everything that happened is the perfect note to end on — nothing has been learned, the social machinery just rolls forward. The morning-after normality is itself the punchline.

tmdb_overview: Larry's little dinner at home with Arthur, initiated by Jeannie, escalates into a full-blown party and causes Larry to become extremely paranoid.
